claims.text: A coherent BCC-rich phase enriched in Ti and Fe can be formed within an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix.
Formation of the Ti/Fe-enriched BCC phase will induce local chemical segregation.
Ti/Fe chemical segregation will enhance the orbital magnetic moment.
The secondary BCC-rich phase will create domain-wall pinning sites.
The proposed BCC-rich phase and associated pinning will raise coercivity above 100 Oe while retaining magnetic ordering significantly above room temperature.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti has coercivity below approximately 20 Oe.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti has suppressed orbital moments.
Co-Cu-Fe-Ni-Zn films exhibit soft-magnetic behavior with a coercivity of 19.5 Oe.
Uniform chemical composition in Co-Cu-Fe-Ni-Zn causes low magnetic anisotropy.
Adjusting Ti content and Fe/Co ratios in Fe-Co-Ni-Ti will trigger nanoscale chemical separation into fcc and BCC-rich regions.
Al addition to FeMnCoCrAl can induce a BCC phase, including a single BCC solid solution at 8 at.% Al.
Co-Cu-Fe-Ni-Zn provides an established example of FCC/BCC dual-phase formation.
Sputtering below 80 degrees Celsius can stabilize the proposed dual-phase Fe-Co-Ni-Ti structure.
FCC/BCC nanoscale phase boundaries act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Ti/Fe segregation modifies the electronic density of states and restores orbital-moment contributions.
The Ti/Fe-rich BCC phase introduces lattice distortion and chemical disorder that generate local magnetic anisotropy.
Local anisotropy and pinning impede domain-wall motion and thereby increase coercivity.
The dual-phase alloy will retain high saturation magnetization comparable to single-phase BCC or FCC systems.
The dual-phase alloy will have a Curie temperature above 900 K inherited from BCC phase stability.
Coercivity enhancement requires a coherent BCC phase smaller than 20 nm, while growth beyond 50 nm will reduce coercivity by lowering pinning-site density.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires Tc above 900 K, but the falsification rule rejects only Tc below room temperature. A measured Tc between room temperature and 900 K would fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the given rule.
